Ingenious

in-JEEN-yus -- not to be confused with 'ingenuous,' meaning innocent or naive. · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Ingenious is clever, original, and inventive.

The engineers devised an ingenious solution that used half the material at twice the strength.

Worked Example

A student with no money for a science fair budget builds a working water filter entirely out of a plastic bottle, sand, and charcoal, and it outperforms every store-bought model in the competition.

That clever, original problem-solving is exactly what ingenious describes. Unlike 'expensive,' which describes cost, ingenious describes clever, resourceful thinking.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

clever: quick to understand and having original ideas

inventive: having the ability to create new things or ideas

resourceful: able to find quick and clever ways to solve problems

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

unimaginative: lacking creativity or original ideas

clumsy: lacking skill or grace; awkwardly done

Where it sits · how original the thinking is — clever → ingenious → inventive

clever vs. ingenious: Clever is a broader, more everyday word than ingenious -- clever can describe any quick or witty idea, while ingenious specifically emphasizes originality and inventive problem-solving.

inventive vs. ingenious: Inventive can feel even stronger than ingenious in one sense: ingenious often praises how cleverly a specific problem was solved, while inventive emphasizes the broader ability to keep creating new things.

Build the Word

The pieces

prefix — in-

prefix — in-: in, within (Latin)

root — -gen-

root — -gen-: to create, produce, beget (Latin (gignere, ingenium))

suffix — -ious

suffix — -ious: full of, having the quality of (Latin (-osus))

Put it together

Put it together: Latin in- ('within') plus gignere ('to create, produce') built ingenium, 'inborn talent,' and the ending -ious ('full of') finishes the word. An ingenious mind is full of that inborn knack for creating clever new solutions.

Use the root in a new word: generate

Use the root in a new word: generate: The old windmill could generate just enough electricity to power the farmhouse's lights.
